title: Two Small Secrets To Cold Call Success
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov identifies two underused Cold Call refinements from a 2014 classroom video of Troy Prep teacher Dave Javsicas that make the technique feel more natural, conversational, and motivating for students. The first refinement, "Polling," involves asking students to signal readiness before being named -- dramatically lowering the social stakes of Cold Call because the teacher already has evidence the student has an idea. The second, "Norm Amplification," leverages peer approval as the most powerful positive reinforcer available in a classroom: after a student answers, the teacher asks how many others thought similarly, making peer agreement visible and legible to the respondent. Together, these moves transform Cold Call from an anxiety-inducing spotlight into an inclusive, participation-building tool that rewards thinking rather than penalizing uncertainty. Lemov notes he uses analogous norm-amplification phrases in adult professional development contexts with equal effect.
points: * Polling before Cold Call -- 'How many people have at least one idea down?' -- converts the technique from a cold spotlight to a warm follow-up, because the teacher calls on students who have already signaled they have thought productively about the question. * Norm Amplification exploits the research finding that peer approval is more influential than teacher praise: asking 'How many people had something like that?' after a student answers makes classmates' agreement visible and is a powerful incentive to speak again. * Lemov's two preferred Norm Amplification phrases -- 'I see lots of people nodding their heads' and 'I see lots of people writing that down' -- are deliberately factual and low-key, drawing the speaker's attention to real signals without fabricating approval. * The Polling technique doubles as a formative assessment move: by asking students to keep hands up from 'one idea' to 'two ideas,' the teacher gets a real-time snapshot of how much thinking has occurred before calling on anyone. * Both techniques shift Cold Call's social logic -- from 'will I look foolish if I don't know?' to 'I've already shown I have something to say' -- which is especially important for building participation habits in reluctant or anxious students.
quotes: Dave gives his students a bit of time to write brief responses to a poem they've just read. Then he says: 'How many people have at least one idea down?' Students raise their hands. 'Great. Keep your hands up if you have at least two ideas down.'

He's basically said: 'Who has an answer or an idea right now?' When students raise their hands, it's now doubly-easy to call on them. 'Great. Juan tell us what you wrote about...' Dave here starts with Kamari and it's easy to do because she's already signalled to him that she's thought productively about the question and has ideas.

After Kamari gives her answer, Dave says, 'How many people had something like that?' Lots of kids raise their hands. The result is that Kamari instantly sees that people thought similarly and agreed with her. Dave is amplifying her perception of peer agreement and approval and this is very powerful as it makes her feel successful after responding, like she added something valid to the discussion.

It's good if Dave says, 'Hmmm, Kamari, what a good idea,' but we know that a student's perception of her peers' approval is much more influential. Dave is making that approval more legible to her: Look at all the people who agree with you!

I use a version of this move all the time with adult participants in professional development, and I especially rely on two Norm Amplification phrases that I think are eminently copy-able. After someone gives an answer I say: 'Hmm. I see lots of people nodding their heads' or 'Hmmm. I see lots of people writing that down.'

In both cases I am merely drawing the speaker's attention to the fact that other people in the room valued what they said, and this is a strong incentive to speak again and to believe, accurately, that they added value.
Once you have that signal: I've thought about it; I have an opinion, the Cold Call feels doubly inviting. This makes the Cold Call feel natural, conversational and inclusive.
